intro: This is the first movement, marked Vivace, of Haydn’s String Quartet in C major, Op. 54 No. 2, Hob. III:57, played by the Danish String Quartet. The first violin opens in C major, and Haydn then stops all four players with rests.

sections.label: A · C major theme with rests
sections.mNote: The first violin’s opening phrase breaks off several times.

sections.label: Dev · The violin phrase travels
sections.mNote: The opening returns loudly over changed harmony.

sections.label: A′ · Opening theme in C major
sections.mNote: The cello’s A♭ returns beneath the first violin.

cues.title: Five-bar phrases and general pauses
cues.text: The first violin plays a phrase above held notes, and then the whole quartet stops. Haydn writes phrases five bars long and pauses for all four players, so the silences also fall outside a regular four-bar pattern.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, opening page. Laurie Shulman identifies irregular five-bar phrases and dramatic pauses: https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Johann Tost in Paris, 1788
cues.text: Johann Tost left the Esterházy orchestra in 1788 and took six new Haydn quartets to Paris, among them Op. 54. He arranged their publication with Sieber, and his name has stayed attached to the music.
cues.evidence: Laurie Shulman, programme note, p. 2: Tost’s departure, Paris visit and publication arrangements for Opp. 54 and 55. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: Opening of the development
cues.text: After the close in G major, the first violin restates its opening phrase loudly. The lower strings change the chords beneath it, and the development takes the figure through new keys.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, end of exposition and opening of development, pp. 182–184. Peter Holman discusses the movement’s sharp changes of key: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/notes/66971-B.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recapitulation in C major
cues.text: The first violin restates its opening phrase in C major. Beneath it the cello’s A♭ returns, as at the start, so Haydn brings back the interruption with the theme.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace: opening and recapitulation, including the A♭ bass beneath the restated phrase.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Rosemary Hughes on the first violin
cues.text: The first violin has an unusually prominent role in all twelve Tost quartets. Rosemary Hughes considered this quartet’s first movement the best example, “with its bold, striding gestures and big sonorities”, and wrote that the virtuosity gives the music “fire and eloquence”.
cues.evidence: Rosemary Hughes on Op. 54 No. 2, quoted in Laurie Shulman’s programme note for the Schumann Quartet, 20 November 2022, p. 2. https://pac.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Schumann-Quartet-program-pages.pdf

cues.title: Second group in C major
cues.text: The second-group tune, marked piano dolce and first heard in G major, returns in C major.
cues.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace: the p dolce second group in G major and its C major return.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Tel Aviv Museum of Art, May 2015
cues.text: The Danish String Quartet played this at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art in May 2015, and the museum’s music channel filmed the concert. Three of the players met as children at a summer camp for amateur musicians, where they played football and chamber music. The Norwegian cellist Fredrik Schøyen Sjölin joined them in 2008.
cues.evidence: Video description from the Tel Aviv Museum of Art’s music channel: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dGgmFFMFICc. The quartet’s own account, “Our story” (three Danes met at a summer camp for enthusiastic amateur musicians, playing football and chamber music; “In 2008 Norwegian cellist Fredrik joined in”): https://www.danishquartet.com/about ; ECM Records artist page (summer camp; Sjölin joined in 2008): https://ecmrecords.com/artists/danish-string-quartet/ (both opened). The 2008 change of name reported by Wikipedia is not repeated: neither source states it.

transitions.title: End of exposition into development
transitions.from: A · C major theme with rests
transitions.how: The exposition closes quietly in G major. The first violin restarts its opening phrase forte over sustained lower strings. Altered notes in the accompaniment move the harmony away from G, and the opening phrase returns before the music settles in a new key.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, end of exposition and opening of development.

transitions.title: Return of the opening over C and A♭
transitions.to: A′ · Opening theme in C major
transitions.how: The bass holds G, and the first violin then brings back the opening phrase in C major. A few bars later the cello moves to A♭, and the harmony that first sounded beneath that phrase returns.
transitions.evidence: Eulenburg score, edited by Wilhelm Altmann, Vivace, approach to the recapitulation and return of the opening phrase over C and A♭.

composer.epithet: Composer known for an orchestral work in which the players leave one at a time, and for a quartet that continues after listeners think it has ended.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he wrote in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three. He was a wheelwright’s son and had spent most of his adult life in the livery of a servant of the Esterházy family.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. As a chorister he sang church music daily but received little instruction in composition. Performances outside the cathedral also gave him chances to get a meal. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
